figures.name: fig4_critical_difference_accuracy
figures.title: Critical difference diagram (accuracy)
figures.caption: Critical difference diagram over 84 datasets for the 29 models with a complete sweep. Models are placed by average rank (accuracy), best on the left. A thick horizontal bar joins models whose pairwise differences are not statistically significant under a Wilcoxon signed-rank test with Holm correction at $\alpha$=0.05; models sharing a bar cannot be separated by this evidence. Labels read \texttt{encoder\_\_pooling}, abbreviated, where sea\_ marks a component introduced in this work and mil\_ one reused unchanged from MILLET.
figures.question: Which differences in accuracy are statistically significant?
figures.label: fig:fig4_critical_difference_accuracy

figures.name: stats_average_rank_accuracy
figures.title: Average rank (accuracy)
figures.caption: Average accuracy rank of each fully-swept model over 84 datasets (rank 1 is best on a dataset). Ranking is robust to a single easy dataset in a way that a mean is not.
figures.question: Which model is best overall on accuracy, robust to individual datasets?
figures.label: fig:stats_average_rank_accuracy

figures.name: fig5_win_tie_loss_accuracy
figures.title: Win / tie / loss against MILLET (accuracy)
figures.caption: Per-dataset accuracy record of each fully-swept model against the published MILLET results, over the 84 datasets both report. Differences within 0.005 count as ties, since that is below the resolution of these test sets. Sorted by number of wins; the rank prefix uses competition ranking, so models with an equal number of wins share a rank and are marked with '='.
figures.question: How often does each model actually beat the published baseline on accuracy?
figures.label: fig:fig5_win_tie_loss_accuracy

figures.name: stats_improvement_over_millet_accuracy
figures.title: Average improvement over MILLET (accuracy)
figures.caption: Mean per-dataset accuracy difference against the published MILLET results. Green bars improve on the baseline, red bars fall short. Read together with the win/tie/loss figure: this shows the size of the gap, that one shows how often it goes each way.
figures.question: By how much does each model improve on the baseline in accuracy?
figures.label: fig:stats_improvement_over_millet_accuracy

figures.name: stats_pairwise_wins_accuracy
figures.title: Pairwise win matrix (accuracy)
figures.caption: Head-to-head accuracy record over 84 datasets: the cell in row i and column j counts the datasets on which model i beats model j. Models are ordered by average rank, so a well-ordered matrix is green above the diagonal.
figures.question: Which models beat which other models directly, rather than on average?
figures.label: fig:stats_pairwise_wins_accuracy

figures.name: appendix_dataset_model_heatmap_accuracy
figures.title: Dataset x model heatmap (accuracy)
figures.caption: Per-dataset accuracy difference from the published MILLET results for every fully-swept model (28 models x 84 datasets). Blue is better than the baseline, red is worse, white is equal. Datasets are ordered by mean difference, so systematic strengths and weaknesses appear as vertical bands. Dataset names are omitted for space; the ordering is in the accompanying CSV.
figures.question: Where do the gains and losses against the baseline actually come from?
figures.label: fig:appendix_dataset_model_heatmap_accuracy

figures.name: appendix_accuracy_distribution
figures.title: Per-dataset accuracy distribution
figures.caption: Distribution of accuracy across 84 datasets for each fully-swept model, ordered by average rank. The box spans the interquartile range and the line is the median, so consistency is visible alongside central tendency. Note that this shows variation across DATASETS: each model was trained once, so these boxes do not represent run-to-run variance.
figures.question: How consistent is each model across datasets, not just on average?
figures.label: fig:appendix_accuracy_distribution

figures.name: stats_metric_correlation
figures.title: Metric correlation
figures.caption: Spearman rank correlation between every reported metric across all evaluated models. Rank correlation is used because what matters is whether two metrics order the models the same way. Values near zero identify genuinely independent axes, which is why they are reported separately rather than combined into one score.
figures.question: Are our metrics measuring different things, or repeating each other?
figures.label: fig:stats_metric_correlation
